title: Israel's election ends without a majority; rallies urge opposition to govern with Arab parties
dek: Netanyahu's bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot's camp 48 and Arab-led parties 19. Rallies on Saturday urged a Jewish-Arab coalition as Likud's interference claims go to the Shin Bet.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Israel faces weeks or months of coalition bargaining after the final count from Tuesday's general election left no camp with a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc won 53 seats, according to final figures from the Central Elections Committee cited in reports. The opposition camp led by Gadi Eisenkot won 48, and Arab-led parties won 19. A government needs 61 seats. The pro-Netanyahu parties held 68 seats in the outgoing Knesset.

## The party picture

Likud remains the largest party with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar with 21, according to reports. B'Yachad won 12, the Joint List 11, and The Democrats and Ra'am eight each. Yisrael Beytenu, United Torah Judaism and Otzma Yehudit took seven each, and Shas and Religious Zionism six each. Turnout was 77.9%, the highest in decades.

Earlier counts had put the Joint List at 12 and Ra'am at seven; the final tally shifted one seat between them.

## Fraud claims rejected

Likud has accused Arab-led parties of having "stolen" the election, possibly with foreign help, reports said, without offering evidence. The committee's chair, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, passed what he called serious suspicions of foreign interference to the Shin Bet security service for investigation, while saying he could not verify them.

The committee's acting director general, Dean Livne, said reports of a stolen election were "entirely unfounded" and that any inquiry would not affect the final results. Police have also said there is no basis for the claims, reports said.

Netanyahu, in his post-election speech, said a government that relied on Arab parties would "endanger Israel", reports said.

## Rallies for a Jewish-Arab government

On Saturday evening, supporters of the opposition held rallies in several cities calling on its leaders to form a government with the Arab-led parties. The organisers, the Jewish-Arab movement Standing Together, said rallies would be held at Habima Square in Tel Aviv, Paris Square in Jerusalem, and in Beersheba, Haifa and Tayibe, according to reports. "Protesters are demanding that the bloc's leaders recognize their victory and form a government based on Jewish-Arab partnership," the organisers said.

Their argument rests on the arithmetic: the opposition parties and the Arab-led parties together hold 67 seats, six more than a majority, while Netanyahu's bloc has 53.

## The interference inquiry

The election committee wants the Shin Bet's findings on alleged foreign interference within a week, reports said. Qatar, which some Likud figures have linked to the claims, called the allegations "ridiculous and dangerous". Ra'am's leader Mansour Abbas welcomed the inquiry and said his party had "nothing to do with the case".

Eisenkot said Likud was making the allegations "because they lost", and Democrats leader Yair Golan accused Netanyahu of trying to undermine the result "through an ugly delegitimization campaign", reports said. President Herzog called it a "sensitive moment" and asked for a full investigation. Eisenkot has said he is open, under conditions, to working with Arab-led parties, and Joint List MK Ahmad Tibi said the opposition had approached him about replacing the Knesset speaker, according to reports.

## What happens next

The official results are due to be presented to President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday, 4 November, after which he will consult party leaders on who should be asked to form a government. Herzog has urged politicians to avoid another election. The new Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on November 10.

Eisenkot has met Naftali Bennett and Yair Golan, and Golan has held talks with Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas, reports said. Ra'am's leader has said a minority government is unlikely. Coalition talks are expected to be difficult and could last more than two months.
